Questions on Notice have been received from Councillor Nicole Mazeika in relation to pothole and minor road repairs (response times, repair standards and Council equipment). 


Questions

CRM response times

  1. What is Council's current target timeframe from the receipt of a pothole or minor road defect through Council's Customer Relationship Management (CRM) system to:

  • assessment of the reported defect;
  • commencement of remedial works; and
  • completion of the repairs 
  
Actual performance against target

  1. Over the past 12 months, what has been the average and median timeframe between a pothole or minor road defect being reported through the CRM system and the repair being completed?
  
Minimum repair standard

  1. What is Council's current minimum technical or quality standard for pothole and minor pavement repairs, including:

  • preparation of the failed area prior to repair;
  • materials used;
  • depth and application of repair material;
  • compaction requirements; and
  • expected durability/lifespan of the repair?
  
Temporary versus permanent repairs

  1. Does Council distinguish between a temporary remedial repair and a permanent pavement repair? If so, what criteria determine which method is used, and what timeframe applies for a temporary repair to be permanently rectified?
  

 

Repair failures

  1. Over the past 12 months, how many pothole or minor road repairs have required a subsequent repair at the same location within 3, 6 or 12 months?
  
Current repair methodology

  1. What methods and materials are currently used by Council staff to undertake pothole and minor pavement repairs, and what proportion of these works are undertaken in-house versus by external contractors?
  
Previous bitumen patching truck

  1. Does Council previously having a dedicated bitumen patching truck provide any historical information regarding:

  • the purchase and operating cost of the vehicle;
  • its annual utilisation;
  • the number of repairs undertaken;
  • the staffing required; and
  • the reasons the vehicle and associated capability were discontinued? 
  
Current capability and equipment

  1. What equipment does Council currently have available for rapid-response pothole and minor pavement repairs, and does Council consider its current equipment sufficient to achieve the required repair standards and response times?
  
Cost comparison

  1. What was Council's total expenditure on pothole and minor pavement repairs during the 2025/26 financial year, including both internal labour/material costs and external contractor expenditure?
  
Future capability

  1. Has Council undertaken any recent assessment of whether purchasing or leasing a dedicated bitumen/asphalt patching truck would improve response times, repair quality and value for money? If not, could officers provide an indicative cost-benefit assessment of reinstating this capability?
 

 



Questions and Answers

CRM response times

  1. What is Council's current target timeframe from the receipt of a pothole or minor road defect through Council's Customer Relationship Management (CRM) system to:
  • assessment of the reported defect;
  • commencement of remedial works; and
  • completion of the repairs 

Council’s current service target is to assess the reported defect and make the location safe within three days. The matter is then forwarded to the relevant team, with the appropriate remedial works targeted for completion within a further 10 days.
 
The intended end-to-end target is therefore up to 13 days from receipt of the CRM request, subject to the nature of the defect, safety priority, site conditions and the repair method required.

Actual performance against target

  1. Over the past 12 months, what has been the average and median timeframe between a pothole or minor road defect being reported through the CRM system and the repair being completed?
 
During the 2025/26 financial year, internal teams completed 477 pothole repair jobs. The median time from a job being opened to being closed was 28 days, and the average was 42 days. Both measures are outside Council’s target response timeframe.
 
Performance was affected by a small number of larger or more complex patches that remained open for an extended period. These works were beyond the scope of the teams’ primary make-safe role and were referred to the appropriate internal team or an external contractor for completion.
 
Reported pothole numbers have also increased significantly compared with previous years. Based on CRM data, community-reported jobs appear to be at least four times higher than earlier reporting levels. Further assessment is underway to understand whether this reflects an actual increase in potholes, changes in community reporting, or whether proactive scoping works have not been as effective in identifying and addressing defects before they become reported issues.
 
Minimum repair standard

  1. What is Council's current minimum technical or quality standard for pothole and minor pavement repairs, including:
  • preparation of the failed area prior to repair;
  • materials used;
  • depth and application of repair material;
  • compaction requirements; and
  • expected durability/lifespan of the repair?
 
For a permanent pothole or minor pavement repair, the failed area should be squared off and the existing pavement removed to the full depth of the failed material. The exposed area is then cleaned and prepared before an approved bonding agent, such as asphalt emulsion, is applied to the vertical and horizontal surfaces.
 
Hot-mix asphalt is placed, levelled and compacted to match the surrounding road surface and provide a uniform, smooth finish. Ambient (cold mix) asphalt requires the same site preparation, although the bonding agent is incorporated into the product.
 
When correctly prepared, placed and compacted, both hot-mix and ambient asphalt repairs are expected to provide a service life of at least five years, subject to pavement condition, traffic loading and site conditions.
 
Hot-mix asphalt can be trafficked once it has cooled and should perform consistently with the surrounding road surface. Ambient asphalt may take up to four days to fully cure, with shorter curing periods in warmer weather. During the initial curing period, straight-line vehicle movements provide additional compaction, while turning movements can disturb or deform the repair.
 
A recent repair was undertaken as an interim hazard treatment pending a larger contractor patch. The location was subject to turning vehicle movements, the ambient asphalt had limited curing time, and the failed area required a more substantial cut-out and compacted repair. These factors contributed to the need for further treatment.

Temporary versus permanent repairs

  1. Does Council distinguish between a temporary remedial repair and a permanent pavement repair? If so, what criteria determine which method is used, and what timeframe applies for a temporary repair to be permanently rectified?
 

Pothole repairs completed to the required preparation and compaction standard are generally considered permanent repairs intended to extend the life of the road asset.

 

The team’s primary focus at the first site visit is to assess the conditions and make the location safe, rather than necessarily complete the permanent repair at that time. Depending on the defect, pavement condition, traffic movements, weather, available materials and the extent of the failure, the crew may complete a permanent repair during the visit or apply a temporary make-safe treatment and refer the site for further works.

 

Where the broader road surface is significantly degraded, including extensive crazing or cracking, an individual pothole repair may be treated as an interim risk-control measure because the road requires a larger patch or renewal treatment. The crew assesses the site and determines whether a localised pothole repair or a larger pavement patch is appropriate.

 

The timeframe for the larger treatment depends on the severity of the defect, road safety risk, available funding, program priority and contractor or internal resource availability.

 
Repair failures

  1. Over the past 12 months, how many pothole or minor road repairs have required a subsequent repair at the same location within 3, 6 or 12 months?


Council reviewed 477 pothole and minor road repairs completed in 2025/26 to estimate how often repaired locations needed further attention. Based on CRM records, the review indicates that about 40 repairs, or 8%, may have required follow-up within three months; about 65, or 14%, within six months; and about 90, or 19%, within 12 months.

 

Repeat issues were concentrated at a relatively small number of locations and may have been influenced by ageing road surfaces, utility trenches, drainage or water damage, heavy traffic and the use of temporary repairs. These figures are estimates based on CRM records and recurring reports.

 
Current repair methodology

  1. What methods and materials are currently used by Council staff to undertake pothole and minor pavement repairs, and what proportion of these works are undertaken in-house versus by external contractors?
 

Council uses both hot-mix asphalt and ambient (cold mix) asphalt for pothole and minor pavement repairs. Hot-mix asphalt was previously delivered using a dedicated patching truck. Ambient asphalt is supplied in pre-prepared bags, allowing multiple crews to undertake repairs. Both products require the failed area to be properly prepared and the repair material to be effectively compacted.

 

In 2025/26, internal teams completed 477 pothole or patch jobs and contractors completed eight larger patches. Based on job numbers, approximately 98.4% of repairs were completed internally and 1.6% by contractors.

 

The contractor work covered approximately 350 square metres across eight jobs. These were larger or more complex works that the internal team did not have the capability to undertake at the time.

 
Previous bitumen patching truck

  1. Does Council previously having a dedicated bitumen patching truck provide any historical information regarding:
  • the purchase and operating cost of the vehicle;
  • its annual utilisation;
  • the number of repairs undertaken;
  • the staffing required; and
  • the reasons the vehicle and associated capability were discontinued? 
 

The indicative purchase price for an asphalt patching truck, depending on specification and attachments (including spreader bars, side conveyors and emulsion heaters) will most likely exceed $500,000.

 

The previous operating model assumed the asphalt team could manage its workload over two to three days each week. In practice, staff absences, leave and redirection to other operational priorities reduced the number of days available for asphalt patching work. Historical utilisation of the asphalt patching truck was low, and even with the recent increase in reported jobs, the utilisation of a dedicated $500,000 vehicle would likely remain relatively low.

 

The dedicated vehicle was discontinued because its size and cost were considered disproportionate to the relatively low volume of pothole and patching work. For context, internal teams completed 477 pothole or patch repairs during 2025/26, or 1.9 per workday (assuming 252 working days in a year).


Current capability and equipment

  1. What equipment does Council currently have available for rapid-response pothole and minor pavement repairs, and does Council consider its current equipment sufficient to achieve the required repair standards and response times?

Pothole work is currently shared between the Rapid Response teams and the Asphalt team. Ambient asphalt is used at most pothole locations, with an emphasis on straight sections of road where the product can cure without being disturbed by turning vehicles. Passing traffic also provides additional compaction and increases the life of the repair.

 

The team is now using a trailer capable of carrying approximately one tonne of hot-mix asphalt under a heat-resistant cover. Early use of this arrangement has been positive. The trailer allows crews to complete somewhat larger patches and undertake repairs in locations where turning vehicle movements are unavoidable.

 

Contractors can also be engaged for potholes or larger asphalt patches where internal capacity, equipment or capability is insufficient.

 

The current equipment can achieve the required repair standard when the correct preparation, material selection and compaction methods are followed. However, the 28-day median completion time indicates that current resourcing, work prioritisation and available delivery windows have not consistently achieved the response-time target.

 
Cost comparison

  1. What was Council's total expenditure on pothole and minor pavement repairs during the 2025/26 financial year, including both internal labour/material costs and external contractor expenditure?
 

Based on the available figures, Council’s indicative expenditure on pothole and minor pavement repairs during 2025/26 was approximately $350,000, excluding GST. This comprised about $75,000 for eight contractor jobs covering about 350 square metres, about $25,000 for hot-mix asphalt, about $100,000 in internal labour, and an indicative historical operating cost of about $150,000 for the previous asphalt truck, including fuel, maintenance and insurance. These figures are estimates drawn from available system and operational records and are intended to provide an indicative cost comparison rather than an audited cost statement.

 
Future capability

  1. Has Council undertaken any recent assessment of whether purchasing or leasing a dedicated bitumen/asphalt patching truck would improve response times, repair quality and value for money? If not, could officers provide an indicative cost-benefit assessment of reinstating this capability?
 

Council has not completed a recent formal cost-benefit assessment for purchasing or leasing a dedicated bitumen/asphalt patching truck.

 

At this stage, the preferred approach is to use lower-cost improvements to internal capability before considering a significant investment in a dedicated patching vehicle. Council is currently using a ute and hot-mix trailer package, which allows crews to undertake larger or higher-quality repairs than ambient asphalt alone, while retaining flexibility across existing teams. The package also provides broader operational benefit, as the ute and trailer can be used for other field activities when pothole demand is lower, without materially reducing the team’s pothole response capability.

 

Based on current information, reinstating a dedicated patching truck would require a substantial capital investment, likely to be more than $500,000 depending on specification, as well as ongoing operating, maintenance, fuel, material and staffing costs. The value for money of that investment would depend on whether Council has enough consistent asphalt repair work to fully utilise the vehicle and whether it would materially improve response times, repair durability and reliance on contractors.  At the current pothole reporting rate of under 2 potholes reported per workday, it is unlikely that a significant investment in a dedicated asphalt patching truck will represent the best use of Council capital and operational funding.

 

The current ute and trailer arrangement will provide practical evidence on repair quality, response times, crew productivity and the remaining need for contractor support. Council is also testing the market to understand available equipment options, costs and delivery models before any future investment decision is made. Once the arrangement has been assessed against actual demand and repair outcomes, Council will be better placed to determine whether a dedicated patching truck would provide sufficient operational and financial benefit.

The trailer allows crews to complete somewhat larger patches and undertake repairs in locations where turning vehicle movements are unavoidable.

 

Contractors can also be engaged for potholes or larger asphalt patches where internal capacity, equipment or capability is insufficient.

 

The current equipment can achieve the required repair standard when the correct preparation, material selection and compaction methods are followed. However, the 28-day median completion time indicates that current resourcing, work prioritisation and available delivery windows have not consistently achieved the response-time target.

 
Cost comparison

  1. What was Council's total expenditure on pothole and minor pavement repairs during the 2025/26 financial year, including both internal labour/material costs and external contractor expenditure?
 

Based on the available figures, Council’s indicative expenditure on pothole and minor pavement repairs during 2025/26 was approximately $350,000, excluding GST. This comprised about $75,000 for eight contractor jobs covering about 350 square metres, about $25,000 for hot-mix asphalt, about $100,000 in internal labour, and an indicative historical operating cost of about $150,000 for the previous asphalt truck, including fuel, maintenance and insurance. These figures are estimates drawn from available system and operational records and are intended to provide an indicative cost comparison rather than an audited cost statement.

 
Future capability

  1. Has Council undertaken any recent assessment of whether purchasing or leasing a dedicated bitumen/asphalt patching truck would improve response times, repair quality and value for money? If not, could officers provide an indicative cost-benefit assessment of reinstating this capability?
 

Council has not completed a recent formal cost-benefit assessment for purchasing or leasing a dedicated bitumen/asphalt patching truck.

 

At this stage, the preferred approach is to use lower-cost improvements to internal capability before considering a significant investment in a dedicated patching vehicle. Council is currently using a ute and hot-mix trailer package, which allows crews to undertake larger or higher-quality repairs than ambient asphalt alone, while retaining flexibility across existing teams. The package also provides broader operational benefit, as the ute and trailer can be used for other field activities when pothole demand is lower, without materially reducing the team’s pothole response capability.

 

Based on current information, reinstating a dedicated patching truck would require a substantial capital investment, likely to be more than $500,000 depending on specification, as well as ongoing operating, maintenance, fuel, material and staffing costs. The value for money of that investment would depend on whether Council has enough consistent asphalt repair work to fully utilise the vehicle and whether it would materially improve response times, repair durability and reliance on contractors.  At the current pothole reporting rate of under 2 potholes reported per workday, it is unlikely that a significant investment in a dedicated asphalt patching truck will represent the best use of Council capital and operational funding.

 

The current ute and trailer arrangement will provide practical evidence on repair quality, response times, crew productivity and the remaining need for contractor support. Council is also testing the market to understand available equipment options, costs and delivery models before any future investment decision is made. Once the arrangement has been assessed against actual demand and repair outcomes, Council will be better placed to determine whether a dedicated patching truck would provide sufficient operational and financial benefit.

Questions on Notice have been received from Councillor Senthil Chidambaranathan in relation to mosquito monitoring and preparedness. 

Questions

Noting the recent rainfall across metropolitan Adelaide and the approaching warmer spring and summer months, can Administration please advise:
 
  1. What mosquito surveillance and monitoring arrangements are currently undertaken by the City of Charles Sturt, including within the Woodville Ward?

  2. How does Council currently identify, monitor and manage potential mosquito breeding locations on Council-managed land, including wetlands, reserves and stormwater infrastructure?

  3. Has Council received mosquito-related complaints in recent years, and have any particular locations, hotspots or trends been identified, including within the Woodville Ward?

  4. What triggers or thresholds are used by Council to determine when additional mosquito monitoring, treatment or other response measures may be required?

  5. What mosquito prevention, monitoring or maintenance activities are currently undertaken at locations considered to present a mosquito breeding risk within the Woodville Ward, including the St Clair Wetlands and relevant stormwater infrastructure?

  6. Are any additional monitoring or preventative maintenance activities planned at known or potential mosquito breeding-risk locations within the Woodville Ward in preparation for the 2026–27 spring and summer period?

  7. What arrangements are in place for Council to coordinate with SA Health and other relevant authorities in the event of a significant increase in mosquito activity or mosquito-borne disease risk?

  8. What community education and communication activities does Council currently undertake, or propose to undertake, regarding mosquito prevention and the management of standing water on private property?

  9. Having regard to recent winter rainfall and the approaching warmer months, does Administration consider Council’s current mosquito surveillance, prevention and response arrangements adequate for the 2026–27 spring and summer period, and are any additional measures being considered?

Questions and Answers

Noting the recent rainfall across metropolitan Adelaide and the approaching warmer spring and summer months, can Administration please advise:
 
  1. What mosquito surveillance and monitoring arrangements are currently undertaken by the City of Charles Sturt, including within the Woodville Ward?

    Council investigates complaints received from the community about potential sources of breeding of mosquitoes. This includes investigating complaints about potential sources of breeding on private property such as neglected swimming or spa pools on private property.
     
  2. How does Council currently identify, monitor and manage potential mosquito breeding locations on Council-managed land, including wetlands, reserves and stormwater infrastructure?

    Due to the complexity of mosquito control, Council does not currently undertake treatment programs in public spaces. Natural mosquito predators, such as the Eastern Gambusia (mosquito eating fish), are present in large numbers across our water systems, including the St Clair Wetland System and provide effective natural management of mosquito numbers. 
Research indicates that stagnant water on private properties is a significant contributor to mosquito breeding, and that Council-managed wetlands are not necessarily the primary source of local mosquito populations. 

  1. Has Council received mosquito-related complaints in recent years, and have any particular locations, hotspots or trends been identified, including within the Woodville Ward?

    Council receives complaints about mosquitoes every year and these are mainly related to potential breeding sources on private properties such as neglected swimming pools and spa pools. Advice will be provided about what action needs to be taken to prevent the water source from being a breeding ground for mosquitoes.

    Council also carries out education mail outs to the community where complaints about mosquitoes are received, but it is unknown what the potential breeding source is.

  2. What triggers or thresholds are used by Council to determine when additional mosquito monitoring, treatment or other response measures may be required?

    SA Health is the lead control agency in SA for outbreaks of serious human mosquito-borne diseases. SA Health provide advice regarding the level of risk that mosquitoes pose, depending on the findings of their surveillance program. As of this month, the level is currently low. SA Health will continue to carry out monitoring and their advice may change.

  3. What mosquito prevention, monitoring or maintenance activities are currently undertaken at locations considered to present a mosquito breeding risk within the Woodville Ward, including the St Clair Wetlands and relevant stormwater infrastructure?

    Council will investigate any concerns reported from the community about any potential mosquito breeding in the St Clair wetland.

    Council partnered with the Adelaide and Mount Lofty Ranges Natural Resources Management Board to engage UniSA to conduct a survey of councils wetlands. The survey found that there were large amounts of wildlife that actively assisted in the control of mosquitoes and that the risk of mosquitoes breeding was low. The program ended in 2019.

  4. Are any additional monitoring or preventative maintenance activities planned at known or potential mosquito breeding-risk locations within the Woodville Ward in preparation for the 2026–27 spring and summer period?

    We don’t have specific preventative maintenance activities for mosquitos as part of our biodiversity and pest management works that occur in reserves or open space. Our programs currently address issues relating to bees and wasps where we remove nests following a customer request. We generally receive guidance and support from other government agencies if there were actions that Council need to perform, and is usually in response to a public health issue.

  5. What arrangements are in place for Council to coordinate with SA Health and other relevant authorities in the event of a significant increase in mosquito activity or mosquito-borne disease risk?

    Every year SA Health has a mosquito subsidy that is available for councils. This subsidy is aimed for high-risk councils eg those located in the Riverland and those that have tidal/salt marshes. SA health does not consider The City of Charles Sturt to be a high-risk council.

  6. What community education and communication activities does Council currently undertake, or propose to undertake, regarding mosquito prevention and the management of standing water on private property?

    SA Health has run an education campaign about mosquitoes for many years called Fight the Bite. Council’s website contains information about mosquitoes, which includes a link to SA Health’s education pamphlet, Fight the Bite.

  7. Having regard to recent winter rainfall and the approaching warmer months, does Administration consider Council’s current mosquito surveillance, prevention and response arrangements adequate for the 2026–27 spring and summer period, and are any additional measures being considered?

    Eastern Gambusia (mosquito eating fish) are present in large numbers across our water systems, including the St Clair Wetland System. While they are an introduced pest species, they do provide some mosquito management benefit by actively feeding on mosquito larvae and other small aquatic organisms. Their established populations can contribute to natural biological control of mosquitoes, particularly in permanent and shallow water areas. However, this benefit needs to be balanced against their impacts on native fish, tadpoles and aquatic invertebrates, and they should not be deliberately introduced or spread for mosquito control.

This report has been prepared to satisfy the requirements of Section 48 of the Local Government Act 1999, which requires that Council obtain and consider a report which addresses Prudential Issues (as defined in the Act) before engaging in a project where the expected capital cost will exceed $4 million (indexed) - currently at $6.147 million.  This report contains information regarding the potential acquisition of land to facilitate the redevelopment/expansion of the Beverley depot.  

 

In accordance with the Local Government Act 1999 the CEO is recommending that this report be heard in confidence under Section 90(3)(b) and (d) as it contains:

(b) information the disclosure of which (i) could reasonably be expected to confer a commercial advantage on a person with whom the council is conducting, or proposing to conduct, business, or to prejudice the commercial position of the council; and (ii) would, on balance, be contrary to the public interest; and

(d) commercial information of a confidential nature (not being a trade secret) the disclosure of which (i) could reasonably be expected to prejudice the commercial position of the person who supplied the information, or to confer a commercial advantage on a third party; and (ii) would, on balance, be contrary to the public interest.

Seconded: Councillor Stuart Ghent

b.

A deputation request was received from Mr Lindsay Holmes on behalf of the Hindmarsh Residents Association Community Archive Group who is requesting to speak to Council regarding the Strategic and Engagement Committee Item 4.1 - Place Naming Project - Methodology Update and Recommended Name Bank.


Moved: Councillor Alice Campbell
Seconded: Councillor Nicholas Le Lacheur

Motion

  1. That the deputation be received and noted. 

  2. That Mr Lindsay Holmes be thanked for his presentation and any notes that comply with Council's Code of Practice for Meeting Procedures and the laws of defamation, be included in the Minutes.
Carried Unanimously

 


That leave of the meeting is sought to hear a presentation for Item 2.2.1 - 4.1 prior to the consideration of the item. Leave was granted.

Moved: Councillor Nicole Mazeika
Seconded: Councillor Quin Tran

4.1. - PRESENTATION - PLACE NAMING PROJECT – METHODOLOGY UPDATE AND RECOMMENDED NAME BANK
 
Motion
 
That the Committee recommends that:
 
  1. Council notes the presentation and update on the Place Naming Project, including work undertaken since Council's consideration of the project on 22 June 2026 and the proposed approach to Kaurna naming as it relates to future place naming within the City of Charles Sturt.
 
  1. Council endorses the amended Place Naming Methodology, as provided in Appendix 2, including the incorporation of a targeted stakeholder feedback stage following the identification of draft names and prior to Council consideration.
 
  1. Council endorses the amended list of recommended place names for the Bowden, Brompton and Hindmarsh area, as detailed in Appendix 3, for use in future naming of roads, reserves and public places.
 
  1. Council notes that staff will undertake follow-up implementation actions, including providing the endorsed list of recommended place names to MAB Corporation to support selection of names for future stages of the Gasworks Brompton development and communicating the outcomes of the Place Naming Project to participating stakeholders.
Carried Unanimously

The City of Charles Sturt acknowledges and pays respect to the traditional custodians of the land, the Kaurna people of the Adelaide plains. We pay our respect to Elders past, present and emerging. We respect their spiritual beliefs and connections to land which are of continuing importance to the Kaurna people of today. We acknowledge the contributions and important role that Aboriginal people continue to play within our local community in Charles Sturt. We also respect the culture of Aboriginal people visiting from other areas of South Australia and Australia.

Almighty Father from Whom all goodness flows, grant unto us qualities of wisdom justice and tolerance, that we the civic leaders of this community may govern in harmony and concord.

This we ask in Thy name. 

We also remember and give thanks for those, our sons and daughters, who gave their lives for Australia. 

Lest we forget.

The City of Charles Sturt acknowledges and pays respect to the traditional custodians of the land, the Kaurna people of the Adelaide plains. We pay our respect to Elders past, present and emerging. We respect their spiritual beliefs and connections to land which are of continuing importance to the Kaurna people of today. We acknowledge the contributions and important role that Aboriginal people continue to play within our local community in Charles Sturt. We also respect the culture of Aboriginal people visiting from other areas of South Australia and Australia.

Almighty Father from Whom all goodness flows, grant unto us qualities of wisdom justice and tolerance, that we the civic leaders of this community may govern in harmony and concord.

This we ask in Thy name. 

We also remember and give thanks for those, our sons and daughters, who gave their lives for Australia. 

Lest we forget.

The Strategic and Engagement Committee was held on Monday, 21 September 2026.


Moved: Councillor Nicole Mazeika
Seconded: Councillor Peter Ppiros

That having considered the recommendations of the Committee which has read and considered the reports in the agenda related to items:

 

4.1. - PRESENTATION - ROWING SA - ORGANISATIONAL OVERVIEW & FUTURE PLANS 
 
Motion
 

That the Committee recommends to the Council:

 

  1.  That the Rowing SA representatives be thanked for their presentation.

 

  1. That the report and Rowing SA's presentation be received and noted, with the presentation to be included as an attachment to the minutes of the meeting.
 
4.2. - ALBERT PARK PLACE NAMING PROJECT
 
Motion 
 

That the Committee recommends to the Council that:

 

  1. Council endorses the road names Gadsden and Fletcher for use within The Gadsden development at 24-30 Murray Street, Albert Park.

 

  1. Council endorses the Albert Park Name Bank contained in Appendix 3 for future place naming opportunities within Albert Park, including roads, reserves, buildings and other public places.

  2. The developer (Rivergum Homes) of The Gadsden development be invited to select the remaining two required road names from the endorsed Albert Park Name Bank.

4.3. - CONSENT TO PLANS OF DIVISION - HOLBROOKS ROAD, EAST AVENUE, GRANGE ROAD INTERSECTION UPGRADE
 
Motion 
 

That the Committee recommends to the Council:

 

  1. That Council accepts the vesting of the public roads shown as Lots 11 and 12 in Deposited Plan 139480, Lots 181 and 182 in Deposited Plan 135627, Lots 52, 53, 54 and 55 in Deposited Plan 139327 and Lots 50 and 51 in Deposited Plan 139442, as shown in Appendix 1.

 

  1. That Council delegates authority to the Chief Executive Officer to sign and deal with all documents necessary to give effect to the vesting of the public roads identified in Recommendation 1 and the associated plans of division, as shown in Appendix 2.

4.4. - LAND PURCHASE FOR ROAD WIDENING - ROSETTA STREET, WEST CROYDON
 
Motion
  

That the Committee recommends to the Council that:

 

  1. Council acknowledge the encroachment of public assets on private land at 71 Rosetta Street, West Croydon as shown in Appendix 1 and resolve to remedy the encroachment through the purchase of approximately 4.6 square metres of Allotment 201 in Deposited Plan 95632 noted in Certificate of Title Volume 6162 Folio 758 as shown in Appendix 2.

 

  1. Council pay to the Registered Proprietor of 71 Rosetta Street, West Croydon $7,500 excluding GST being the market valuation (Appendix 3) of the portion of land as shown in Appendix 2.

 

  1. Council pay to the Registered Proprietor of 71 Rosetta Street, West Croydon $1,500 including GST to cover their legal, conveyancing and valuation expenses incurred as a consequence of the encroachment and purchase of the portion of land as shown in Appendix 2.

  2. The Mayor and Chief Executive Officer be delegated authority to sign, seal and deal with all documents to deliver this resolution.

  

4.5. - COUNCIL ASSESSMENT PANEL JUNE 2026 END OF QUARTER REPORT
 
Motion
  
That the Committee recommends to Council that:
 
  1. The report be received and noted.

Council adopts the recommendations of the Committee as printed in the Minutes of this Committee.


Carried Unanimously

The Operations Committee was held on Monday, 21 September 2026.


Moved: Councillor Senthil ChidambaranathanSeconded: Councillor Stuart Ghent

That having considered the recommendations of the Committee which has read and considered the reports in the agenda related to items:

 

4.1. - GRANT ACCEPTANCE - STATE GOVERNMENT ELECTION COMMITMENTS PROGRAM
 
Motion 
 
That the Committee recommends to Council:
 
  1. That the report be received and noted.
 
  1. That Council accepts the grant funding offers from the Office for Recreation, Sport and Racing under the 2025-26 Election Commitments Program for:             
  1. Sam Johnson Reserve scoreboard replacement - $100,000;
  2. Matheson Reserve sports lighting upgrade - $200,000;
  3. Western Strikers Soccer Club facility redevelopment - $2,000,000; and
  4. Henley & Grange Memorial Oval facility redevelopment - $3,000,000.
 
  1. That the Chief Executive Officer be authorised to execute all documentation necessary to give effect to the grant agreements.
 
4.2. - GRANT ACCEPTANCE - TRIMMER PARADE DRAINAGE UPGRADE PROJECT - STAGES 1 AND 2  
 
Motion 
 
That the Committee recommends to the Council:
 
  1. That Council accepts grant funding of up to $2,000,000 from the Stormwater Management Authority for the Trimmer Parade Drainage Upgrade Project - Stages 1 and 2, subject to the terms and conditions of the grant funding agreement.
 
  1. That Council enters into the formal grant funding agreement with the Stormwater Management Authority and authorises the Chief Executive Officer to execute all documents necessary to give effect to the agreement and receive the grant funding.

4.3. - CITY OPERATIONS CAPITAL WORKS & OPERATING PROGRAM VARIATIONS
 
Motion
  

That the Committee recommends to the Council: 

 

  1. That the following variations to the Capital Works Program or Annual Operating Program be approved and adjusted in the Financial Statements at the next quarterly review as they involve transfers between renewal and new/upgrade works and or new projects to be funded by unbudgeted income:

 

  1. Budgeted expenditure for Football Park - New Open Space (Project 3682 - New) increased by $150,000 from reallocated funds within the Bridge Renewal Seaview Road Underpass RTLP (Project 3623 - Renewal).

 

  1. That the following variations to the Capital Works Program be approved and budgets or scope adjusted accordingly:

 

  1. Scope change to Ray Street Reserve - New Shelter and Seating (3979) with no change to the overall project budget.

 

  1. That by endorsing the variations listed in 1. above, Council is endorsing a variation to the approved Asset Management Plan renewal schedule where relevant.
 
4.4. - TREE LOCATED ADJACENT 38 FLINDERS PARADE, FLINDERS PARK – AMENITY IMPROVEMENTS
 
Motion
 
  1. That the Committee recommends to Council that the report is received and noted.

 

Council adopts the recommendations of the Committee as printed in the Minutes of this Committee.


Carried Unanimously

To seek Council’s endorsement of the 2027 Council and Committee meeting schedule to early May 2027, reflecting the timing of the 2027 Local Government Elections, and to outline the 2027/28 budget development process.



Moved: Councillor Alice Campbell
Seconded: Councillor Michael McEwen

Motion

  1. That Council endorse the Council and Committee meeting schedule for 2027 up until early May, as outlined in Appendix 1.

  2. That Council endorse the Council Assessment Panel 2027 meeting dates as outlined in Appendix 1. 

  3. That the timetable in Appendix 2 be used as the basis for development of the 2027/28 budget.

  4. That the consultation process as described within the report be adopted including the use of online and written submission facilities and the opportunity for community members and groups to make in person deputations to Council. That these opportunities be advertised via Social Media, Council’s website as part of the Rates Notices mailout and Port Road Banners.

  5. That the Draft Annual Business Plan community consultation session proposed for 20 April 2027 from 3.30pm to 5.00pm, have the time changed to 4pm to 6pm.

The Operations Committee was held on Monday, 21 September 2026 and considered Item 9.1 - Property Acquisition Update. The brief of this item is provided as follows:

This report seeks to exclude the purchase of properties from classification as Community Land under section 193 of the Local Government Act 1999 (SA). 

In accordance with the Local Government Act 1999 the CEO is recommending that this report be heard in confidence under Section 90(3)(b) and 90(3)(d) as it contains information the disclosure of which (i) could reasonably be expected to confer a commercial advantage on a person with whom the council is conducting, or proposing to conduct, business, or to prejudice the commercial position of the council; and (ii) would, on balance, be contrary to the public interest. It also contains commercial information of a confidential nature (not being a trade secret) the disclosure of which (ii) could reasonably be expected to prejudice the commercial position of the person who supplied the information, or to confer a commercial advantage on a third party; and (ii) would, on balance, be contrary to the public interest.



Moved: Councillor Edgar Agius
Seconded: Councillor Senthil Chidambaranathan

Recommendation - Exclusion of the Public (from 7:43 PM)
That:
  1. Pursuant to Section 90(2) of the Local Government Act 1999, Council hereby orders that the public be excluded from attendance at this meeting, with the exception of the Chief Executive Officer, General Manager Corporate Services, General Manager City Operations, General Manager City Futures, General Manager Engaged Community, Manager City Property and Open Space, Manager Financial Services, Manager City Planning and Sustainability, Manager Community Engagement and Experience, Manager Performance, Business Intelligence and Improvement, Manager City Utilities, Acting Manager City Infrastructure, Coordinator Place Making, Senior Policy Planner, Governance Officer, PMO Delivery Lead, and Performance and PMO Support Officer currently in attendance at the meeting, in order to consider ITEM 12.1 - OPERATIONS COMMITTEE ITEM 9.1 - PROPERTY ACQUISITION UPDATE in confidence.

  2. In accordance with Section 90(3) of the Local Government Act 1999, Council is satisfied that it is necessary that the public be excluded to consider the information contained in the report ITEM 12.1 - OPERATIONS COMMITTEE ITEM 9.1 - PROPERTY ACQUISITION UPDATE on the following grounds:
b.
information the disclosure of which (i) could reasonably be expected to confer a commercial advantage on a person with whom the council is conducting, or proposing to conduct, business, or to prejudice the commercial position of the council; and (ii) would, on balance, be contrary to the public interest.
d.
commercial information of a confidential nature (not being a trade secret) the disclosure of which (i) could reasonably be expected to prejudice the commercial position of the person who supplied the information, or to confer a commercial advantage on a third party; and (ii) would, on balance, be contrary to the public interest.

  1. Accordingly, on this basis, the principle that meetings of the Council should be conducted in a place open to the public has been outweighed by the need to keep the information or discussion confidential.

The Strategic and Engagement Committee was held on Monday, 21 September 2026 and considered Item 9.3 - Semaphore Park Renewal Precinct - Strategic Opportunity. The brief of this item is provided as follows:

This report provides an overview of the strategic opportunities associated with the Semaphore Park Precinct, which forms part of a State Significant Infill Investigation Area identified in the Greater Adelaide Regional Plan. It seeks to ensure Council is informed early and positioned to collaborate with and advocate to the State Government and respond appropriately to any future private-sector planning processes, to achieve outcomes that respond to local community needs.

In accordance with the Local Government Act 1999 the CEO is recommending that this report be heard in confidence under Section 90(3)(b)(i) and (ii), and (m) as it contains information the disclosure of which (i) could reasonably be expected to confer a commercial advantage on a person with whom the council is conducting, or proposing to conduct, business, or to prejudice the commercial position of the council; and (ii) would, on balance, be contrary to the public interest. It also contains information relating to a proposal to prepare or amend a designated instrument under Part 5 Division 2 of the Planning, Development and Infrastructure Act 2016 before the draft instrument or amendment is released for public consultation under that Act.

Seconded: Councillor Edgar Agius

  2. In accordance with Section 90(3) of the Local Government Act 1999, Council is satisfied that it is necessary that the public be excluded to consider the information contained in the report ITEM 12.4 - STRATEGIC AND ENGAGEMENT COMMITTEE ITEM 9.3 - SEMAPHORE PARK RENEWAL PRECINCT - STRATEGIC OPPORTUNITY on the following grounds:

b.
information the disclosure of which (i) could reasonably be expected to confer a commercial advantage on a person with whom the council is conducting, or proposing to conduct, business, or to prejudice the commercial position of the council; and (ii) would, on balance, be contrary to the public interest.

information relating to a proposal to prepare or amend a designated instrument under Part 5 Division 2 of the Planning, Development and Infrastructure Act 2016 before the draft instrument or amendment is released for public consultation under that Act.

The Audit and Risk Committee was held on Wednesday, 30 September 2026.


Moved: Councillor Nicholas Le Lacheur
Seconded: Councillor Michael McEwen

That having considered the recommendations of the Committee which has read and considered the reports in the agenda related to items:

 

4.1. - BUILD BIG, BID SMART – ALLIANCE DELIVERY MODEL AND GOVERNANCE RISK REVIEW

 

Motion

 

That the Audit and Risk Committee recommends that Council:

 

  1. Receives and notes the independent BRM Advisory Cross Council Alliance – BBBS Delivery Model and Governance Assessment contained in Appendix 1.

 

  1. Notes that the purpose of the BRM Advisory assessment is to provide an independent review of the proposed Alliance delivery model, governance framework, risk environment and implementation considerations, and that it is not an endorsement of the Alliance methodology.

 

  1. Notes BRM Advisory’s assessment that sufficient due diligence has been undertaken to understand how the proposed Alliance is intended to operate and its potential benefits, risks and implementation requirements, while recognising that the final commercial arrangements and contract remain to be refined and finalised with the preferred Alliance partner.

 

  1. Provides the following feedback to Administration for consideration as the procurement, commercial arrangements, governance framework and risk controls continue to be developed: 

a. That the covering report include the six risk mitigation areas matched to the six BRM key risk areas.

b. To note that the risk appetite and tolerance levels across the Councils are aligned.

  

4.2. - DATA GOVERNANCE FRAMEWORK

 

Motion 
 
That the Audit and Risk Committee recommends to Council:

 

  1. That the Data Governance Framework be received and noted.

  

4.3. - ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI) UPDATE

 

Motion 
 
That the Audit and Risk Committee recommends to Council:

 

  1. That the report be received and noted.

  

4.4. - INTERNAL AUDIT REPORT - WORKPLAN UPDATE

 

Motion 
 
That the Audit and Risk Committee recommends to Council:

 

  1. That the report be received and noted.

  

4.5. - INTERNAL AUDIT REPORT - STORMWATER REVIEW

 

Motion 

 

That the Audit and Risk Committee recommends to Council:

 

  1. That the report be received and noted.

 

 4.6. - INTERNAL AUDIT REPORT - REGULATORY COMPLIANCE

 

Motion 
  
 That the Audit and Risk Committee recommends to Council:

 

  1. That the report findings be received and noted.

  

4.7. – INTERNAL AUDIT REPORT – FOLLOW UP OF AGREED HIGH AND EXTREME AUDIT ACTIONS 

 

Motion 
 
That the Audit and Risk Committee recommends to Council:

 

  1. That the report be received and noted.

 

4.8. - INTERNAL AUDIT PROCESSES - CEO ANNUAL REPORT

 

Motion

This report seeks Council endorsement of a response to the State Government’s consultation on proposed reforms to the regulation of Short Stay Accommodation (SSA) in South Australia, collated by the Local Government Association.
 
The proposed reforms include the establishment of a statewide SSA Register, potential introduction of a Code of Conduct and new compliance and enforcement arrangements. The reforms may also introduce new responsibilities for councils, including registration, renewals and aspects of compliance and enforcement.
 
Council’s proposed response is provided at Appendix 1, with the State Government Discussion Paper provided at Appendix 2.

Councillor - Senthil Chidambaranathan entered the meeting at 7:27 PM.

Moved: Councillor Michael McEwen
Seconded: Councillor George Turelli

Motion

That Council:

  1. Submits the proposed response to the State Government’s 'Short Stay Accommodation Register Discussion Paper', as detailed in Appendix 1, to both the LGA and directly to the State Government office of Consumer Business Services.

  2. That for Item 9 in Appendix 1, that the wording be amended with the insertion of 'if possible' after 'financial year 2026/27'.

  3. That Item 1 in Appendix 1 be changed so that only the publicly available information is published rather than the address.
 
Carried Unanimously

On 9 July 2026, the Local Government Association of SA (LGA) wrote to Member Councils calling for nominations for the position of LGA President due to the current membership expiring at the conclusion of the 2026 LGA Annual General Meeting (AGM). At close of nominations on Tuesday, 1 September 2026, four (4) nominations were received from eligible candidates.



Moved: Councillor Senthil ChidambaranathanSeconded: Councillor Edgar Agius

Motion

  1. That Council's voting preference is indicated by placing a "1" next to the candidate that Council wishes to elect as LGA President from the conclusion of the 2026 LGA Annual General Meeting until the conclusion of the 2028 LGA Annual General Meeting, and places consecutive ascending numbers next to all remaining candidates in order of preference:

    2 Mayor Simone Bailey (Mid Murray Council)

    4 Mayor Moira Jenkins (City of Victor Harbor)

    1 Mayor Dean Johnson (District Council of Kimba)

    3 Mayor Leon Stephens (Port Pirie Regional Council)

and the completed ballot nomination is forwarded on to the Local Government Association, in line with the procedure set out in the ballot pack.

Against:Councillor - Merlindie Fardone, Councillor - Katriona Kinsella, Councillor - Michael McEwen, Councillor - Peter Ppiros, Councillor - Kelly Thomas, Councillor - George Turelli (6)
Not Vote:Mayor - Angela Evans (1)
The Motion to Item 6.2. was Carried

A Motion on Notice has been received from Councillor Peter Ppiros requesting that Council reconsider introducing 40 km/h area speed limits on local streets within the area of Kidman Park and Fulham Gardens bounded by Findon Road, Grange Road, Tapleys Hill Road and the River Torrens, and prepare a budget bid for consideration in the 2027/28 Annual Business Plan and Budget.
 
The motion responds to concerns raised with the Councillor about vehicle speeds and unsafe driving behaviour, and requests for lower speed limits following the progressive introduction of 40 km/h areas across the City.

Moved: Councillor Peter PpirosSeconded: Councillor Alice Campbell

Motion 

  1. That Council request the preparation of a budget bid for consideration as part of the 2027/28 Annual Business Plan and Budget for the proposed introduction of 40 km/h area speed limits on local streets within the area of Kidman Park and Fulham Gardens bounded by Findon Road, Grange Road, Tapleys Hill Road and the River Torrens, including provision for community engagement, necessary approvals and installation of signage.

  2. That the outcomes of community engagement and any local roads proposed to be excluded from the 40 km/h area be reported to Council for consideration before proceeding with implementation.

  3. That Councillor Ppiros' notes in relation to this matter be included in the Minutes.

Councillor - Nicholas Le Lacheur left the meeting at 7:55 PM.
Councillor - Senthil Chidambaranathan left the meeting at 8:01 PM.
Councillor - Senthil Chidambaranathan entered the meeting at 8:05 PM.

Leave of the meeting was sought by Councillor Ppiros, with the consent of Councillor Campbell, to vary the motion. Leave was granted.


Moved: Councillor Peter PpirosSeconded: Councillor Alice Campbell

Motion (as Varied)

  1. That Council request the preparation of a budget bid for consideration as part of the 2027/28 Annual Business Plan and Budget for the proposed introduction of 40 km/h area speed limits on local streets within the area of Kidman Park and Fulham Gardens bounded by Findon Road, Grange Road, Tapleys Hill Road and the River Torrens, including provision for community engagement, necessary approvals and installation of signage.

Questions on Notice have been received from Councillor Senthil Chidambaranathan in relation to delayed rubbish bin collections.

Questions

The questions submitted by Councillor Chidambaranathan are in relation to providing an update on emerging trends observed regarding delayed or missed rubbish bin collections. Councillor Chidambaranathan is seeking reassurance that appropriate planning is underway to avoid a recurrence of the collection delays experienced previously. Councillor Chidambaranathan has advised that residents have recently raised concerns regarding delayed rubbish bin collection and that these questions seek to understand whether any emerging risks have been identified and what proactive measures are being undertaken to prevent a recurrence of the collection issues experienced in late 2025 and early 2026.

  1. Are staff seeing any recurring patterns or indicators that suggest we may be heading towards the same issues experienced in late 2025 and early 2026 with missed or delayed collections?
  2. What feedback has Council received from collection contractors regarding service capacity and workforce availability?
  3. As we approach the holiday and Christmas period, what contingency plans are in place to minimise disruptions and ensure residents continue to receive reliable waste collection services?
  4. Are there any additional measures being considered to proactively manage potential service pressures during this peak period?
  5. Can staff provide data on missed and delayed bin collections over the past 60 days, including monthly trends and any identified causes of service interruptions?


Questions and Answers

  1. Are staff seeing any recurring patterns or indicators that suggest we may be heading towards the same issues experienced in late 2025 and early 2026 with missed or delayed collections?

Staff observed a decline in service levels between 14 and 25 September 2026, including an increase in missed services, incomplete collection routes, delays in completing scheduled collections, and resourcing impacts on service delivery. These issues were similar to the service disruptions experienced in late 2025 and early 2026. During this period, repeated failures to complete entire collection routes on the scheduled day resulted in collections being delayed until the following day.

In response to the recent decline in service levels, CAWRA, on behalf of the Councils, issued a further Notice of Direction to the contractor requiring immediate corrective action. The Notice identified ongoing non-compliance with contractual performance standards and directed the contractor to restore reliable service delivery.

  1. What feedback has Council received from collection contractors regarding service capacity and workforce availability?

CAWRA receives daily operational updates from the contractor, including staffing levels, route completion status and outstanding missed collections.

During the fortnight commencing 14 September 2026, staffing levels were below those required to complete all scheduled collection routes on the designated service days. The contractor has advised that reduced driver availability, primarily associated with employee absenteeism, was the principal factor contributing to the delayed collection routes during September. With some days where there were reported 6 drivers absent. The deployment of replacement drivers who are less familiar with particular routes can also contribute to individual missed bins, streets or sections of streets.

This reduction in staffing occurred following a period of relatively consistent service delivery. Following the issuance of the Notice of Direction, the service levels from week beginning 28 September 2026 did improve. At the time of preparing this response, no further incomplete collection routes have been reported since 28 September 2026. CAWRA and Council continue to closely monitor service performance, including missed-bin reports from residents.

  1. As we approach the holiday and Christmas period, what contingency plans are in place to minimise disruptions and ensure residents continue to receive reliable waste collection services?

Council and CAWRA are undertaking proactive planning with the contractor to maintain service continuity over the holiday and Christmas period.

The recently issued Notice of Direction is the formal instrument under the contract that reinforces the contractor's obligations to meet the required service standards and provides a mechanism for CAWRA to require corrective action where those standards are not met. The Notice also enables CAWRA, on behalf of the Councils, to engage alternative contractors and operational resources where necessary to maintain service delivery, with associated costs recoverable from the contractor. These measures provide additional safeguards to minimise the risk of service disruptions during peak demand periods.

  1. Are there any additional measures being considered to proactively manage potential service pressures during this peak period?

Yes. Additional performance monitoring, regular operational reviews, escalation processes, and contingency arrangements are being maintained. CAWRA on behalf of the Councils have also reinforced contractual requirements through the Notice of Direction and retain the ability to implement further interventions should service levels deteriorate. This includes engaging supplementary collection resources if required, to protect service continuity for residents.

 


  1. Can staff provide data on missed and delayed bin collections over the past 60 days, including monthly trends and any identified causes of service interruptions?

The contractor has advised that reduced driver availability, primarily associated with employee absenteeism, was the principal factor contributing to the delayed collection routes during September. The deployment of replacement drivers who are less familiar with particular routes can also contribute to individual missed bins, streets or sections of streets. These shortages can occur daily and are difficult to predict. 
Cleanaway, at times, has had 6 drivers absent on one day.

Questions on Notice have been received from Councillor Senthil Chidambaranathan in relation to 40 km/h area speed limits in the Woodville Ward.


Questions

  1. Which areas of the Woodville Ward are not currently covered by a 40 km/h area speed limit?
  2. When are these remaining areas likely to be considered for a speed limit change?
  3. What process is required to implement a 40 km/h area speed limit on local streets?


Questions and Answers

  1. Which areas of the Woodville Ward are not currently covered by a 40 km/h area speed limit?
The majority of the Woodville Ward is already covered by a 40 km/h area speed limit. As shown on the attached map, Woodville North is the remaining area of the Ward that is not currently included within a 40 km/h area.

Council is proposing to consider Woodville North together with the adjoining suburbs of Pennington and Athol Park as part of the next expansion of the 40 km/h area speed-limit network. Considering these adjoining areas together provides an opportunity to establish a more consistent lower-speed environment across the local street network, with the final extent and boundaries subject to technical assessment, community consultation and relevant DIT requirements.



 

  1. When are these remaining areas likely to be considered for a speed limit change?
Woodville North, Pennington and Athol Park, together with the remainder of Seaton, are proposed to be considered as part of the next expansion of Council's 40 km/h area speed-limit network.

Community consultation is proposed for October 2026, with feedback to be reviewed and considered alongside the technical assessment and relevant DIT requirements. Subject to the outcomes of this process, the necessary approvals and Council endorsement of funding, implementation of the new 40 km/h areas is currently proposed for the 2027/28 financial year.

  1. What process is required to implement a 40 km/h area speed limit on local streets?
Introducing a 40 km/h area speed limit requires Council to assess whether the proposed streets and area boundaries are appropriate for a 40 km/h speed environment in accordance with the DIT Speed Limit Guideline for South Australia and other applicable legislative, road-safety and technical requirements.

For the proposed areas, the process includes technical assessment, community consultation, consideration of feedback, refinement of the proposal where appropriate, Council consideration, obtaining the necessary DIT approvals and, subject to funding, implementation.

As part of the consultation, the community will be able to provide feedback on:

  • their level of support for the proposed 40 km/h area speed limits; 
  • local issues, concerns or opportunities that should be considered before a final decision is made; 
  • streets, intersections or other locations where speeding or road-safety concerns are experienced; 
  • whether the proposed 40 km/h area boundaries are appropriate or whether local adjustments should be considered, subject to technical review; 
  • local knowledge about pedestrian and cycling activity, schools, community facilities and other locations where vulnerable road users may be present; and 
  • local considerations that may need to be taken into account when planning implementation. 

    Community feedback will be considered alongside the technical assessment to inform the final proposal. However, the consultation cannot alter legislative and statutory requirements, engineering and road-safety requirements, applicable standards and DIT requirements or decisions relating to roads or land controlled by DIT or other authorities.
